title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models

paper.title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models.
Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself.
While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher’s supervision at each state affects the student’s learned behavior .
To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior.
Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories.
On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT.
In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses.
More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT.
Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT’s advantage.
These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Distilling a large vision-language model (VLM) into a small one is the standard way to make multimodal reasoning cheap enough to deploy. The common recipe is supervised fine-tuning on teacher-written solutions ( Magister et al., 2023 ; Ho et al., 2023 ) (SFT), which is behavior cloning: the student sees only states the teacher visited, drifts into others at inference, and its errors compound with sequence length ( Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ; Ross et al., 2011 ) . On-policy distillation (OPD) is the DAgger-style remedy ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) : the student samples its own solution, the teacher scores every generated token, and the student minimises a per-token divergence to the teacher on the states it actually reaches. For text-only language models, on-policy distillation on a twentieth of the training set has been reported to outperform supervised distillation on the full set ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , and it is now a standard post-training stage ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . A dense 2026 literature now adapts the objective to VLMs by re-weighting the teacher’s signal toward visually grounded tokens ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026 ) . While these methods change the objective and report the gains of the change, they leave open the question that comes first in practice: given a teacher and a few hundred to a few thousand training questions, when does plain on-policy feedback improve on filtered teacher demonstrations, and which behavior of the teacher does the student acquire along the way? Related work observes that teacher feedback degrades on flawed student prefixes ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) ; our experiments add completion as the behavior at stake, a matched comparison with filtered demonstrations, and a student that loses the completion gain it already had. The two recipes differ in cost and in what they transfer: OPD keeps the teacher in the loop and supervises the student on its own states with whatever the teacher does there; SFT pays once for teacher solutions and transfers only those that survive a correctness filter. Which difference dominates depends on the task, and in our experiments the wrong choice costs up to 7.9 7.9 points. Accuracy at a single budget cannot tell whether a gap comes from the amount of data or the number of training steps, from reasoning errors or from solutions that were never completed, from the objective or from the filter. To investigate these questions, we conducted (Section 2 ) a controlled comparison of the two channels across nested data budgets with each channel’s update count fixed, token-role divergence logging at every training step, and completion diagnostics, applied to a Qwen3-VL 2B student and 8B teacher ( Bai and others, 2025 ) on ChartQA ( Masry et al., 2022 ) and Geometry3K ( Lu et al., 2021 ) . Our contributions are threefold: • A controlled empirical comparison of OPD and filtered SFT. We systematically evaluate both training recipes across four data budgets, four seeds, and two vision-language reasoning tasks with different teacher completion rates. We further examine the sensitivity of their relative performance to SFT training length and evaluation distribution. • Identification of a completion-specific failure mode. We show that final-answer accuracy can obscure substantial differences in completion behavior. By decomposing accuracy differences according to whether each method produces a final answer, we characterize how incomplete responses contribute to the performance gap. We further demonstrate that continued OPD can undo completion behavior previously acquired through SFT. • An empirical investigation of the failure. We examine teacher behavior on student-generated prefixes, compare demonstrations filtered by correctness and completeness, and evaluate five OPD training variants. These analyses characterize the persistence of the completion failure and investigate the possible role of teacher feedback on student-visited states. Two findings stand out. • A persistent failure to complete solutions. On Geometry3K, where the teacher itself does not finish 22% of its solutions within the token budget, OPD students at 900 problems conclude 63% of test responses against 76% for SFT and trail SFT by 7.9 7.9 points ( − 10.5 -10.5 to − 5.3 -5.3 ), of which 6.6 6.6 points come from problems that only one method concludes. OPD started from the SFT student returns its rollout termination rate to plain OPD’s within 40 steps and ends at 62% test completion, the zero-shot level. • A small, non-robust data-efficiency advantage with a reliable teacher. On ChartQA, OPD with 300 training questions reaches 0.826 0.826 accuracy, within 1.4 1.4 points of SFT trained on 3,000 ( 0.840 0.840 ), and leads SFT by 2.7 2.7 points at the same budget under the protocol’s fixed SFT length (per seed + 0.6 +0.6 to + 5.8 +5.8 ) and by 1.1 1.1 to 1.5 1.5 points, with intervals that include zero, against an SFT whose training length is tuned. Together, these results characterize a previously underexplored failure mode of on-policy distillation and give a working rule and a target: on these tasks OPD was competitive with filtered SFT at small budgets only where the teacher reliably completed its solutions; where it did not, the student’s completion failures concentrated on the problems the teacher does not finish, and from those prefixes the teacher rarely concludes, even with the answer in its prompt. Whether that causes the failure or accompanies it awaits a teacher trained to conclude from such states (Section 4.3 ). Our findings motivate evaluating completion alongside accuracy and examining the reliability of teacher feedback on student-visited states.

sections.heading: 2.1 Two supervision channels
sections.text: Let x x be a prompt (an image and a question), π T \pi_{T} the teacher and π θ \pi_{\theta} the student ( Hinton et al., 2015 , distillation as matching the teacher’s outputs,) . SFT samples solutions y ∼ π T ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x) once, keeps those whose final answer is correct ( Ho et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2023 ) , and minimises the token-level cross-entropy − ∑ t log π θ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) -\sum_{t}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) on the kept set. OPD instead samples a batch of rollouts y ( i ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ( i ) ) y^{(i)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x^{(i)}) at every step and minimises the mean, over all generated tokens of the batch, of a divergence between the two next-token distributions on the student’s own prefix, ℒ ( θ ) = 1 ∑ i | y ( i ) | ∑ i ∑ t = 1 | y ( i ) | D ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ( i ) , y < t ( i ) ) ∥ π T ( ⋅ ∣ x ( i ) , y < t ( i ) ) ) , \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sum_{i}|y^{(i)}|}\sum_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{|y^{(i)}|}D\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x^{(i)},y^{(i)}_{<t})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x^{(i)},y^{(i)}_{<t})\big), (1) with D D the reverse KL by default ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . The divergence is taken over the full vocabulary, including the end-of-turn token, at every generated position up to and including the first end-of-turn token or the generation budget; a rollout that runs to the budget contributes every one of its positions. The case for on-policy supervision is DAgger’s ( Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ; Ross et al., 2011 ) : querying the expert on the learner’s own states removes the compounding error of behavior cloning, provided the expert’s action on those states is worth imitating. The two channels therefore differ in two things at once: the states on which the teacher is queried (its own prefixes against the student’s) and the teacher behavior that reaches the student (only correct solutions against everything the teacher does). Our design separates these.

sections.heading: 2.2 Design: what is held fixed and what varies
sections.text: Rather than propose a new objective, we hold everything but the supervision channel and the amount of data fixed: one frozen teacher and one student initialisation, with LoRA on the language-model projections and the vision encoder frozen, so the channels differ in language-side supervision and not in visual representation; one prompt, answer format, generation budget, scorer, and held-out test set per task; budgets that are nested prefixes of one seeded shuffle, so both channels see the same questions and a larger budget adds questions rather than replacing them; and a number of optimizer updates that is fixed within each channel whatever the budget, so that along a curve only the amount of data changes (the counts are not matched between channels; a training-length control on SFT checks this). The teacher is neither prompted for completeness nor retrained: its reliability varies only through the task, and two tasks on which the same teacher is reliable and unreliable turn that dependence into a difference between tasks rather than between teachers. The channel (filtered demonstrations against on-policy token-level feedback) is crossed with four budgets, two tasks, and four paired seeds. Because the channel bundles the state distribution with the filter, two further SFT data sets (no filter; every teacher sample with an answer line, correct or not) separate the two. Five single-component interventions on OPD (the loss on terminated rollouts only, the teacher’s sampling temperature, the forward KL, a sequence-mean loss, initialisation from the SFT student) change one part of the recipe each, and a larger teacher and two out-of-distribution test sets check the dependence on teacher size and test distribution.

sections.heading: 2.3 What we measure
sections.text: Beyond accuracy, three complementary analyses characterize the observed differences and probe possible explanations. Completion diagnostics : a response is complete if it contains an answer line (one without counts as wrong), terminates if it emits the end-of-turn token before the budget, and is truncated if it reaches the budget; paired accuracy differences are decomposed by which method concluded the problem. Feedback logging : at every OPD step we record each generated token’s divergence and a heuristic role ( answer line , numeric value , arithmetic , text ); a role’s KL concentration is its share of the batch’s divergence divided by its share of tokens. Teacher probes : the teacher is continued greedily from prefixes of the student’s truncated and concluded outputs and its end-of-turn probability is read along them, to ask what it does on the student’s states rather than on its own.

sections.heading: Models and tasks.
sections.text: The student is Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, trained with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) of rank 64 on the language-model projections, and the teacher Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct ( Bai and others, 2025 ) , frozen; a 32B teacher is used in Section 4.4 . ChartQA ( Masry et al., 2022 ) is restricted to human-written questions (3,000 training and 500 held-out test questions sampled with a fixed seed), where the 8B teacher answers 84% correctly and concludes 99% of its solutions with an answer line. Geometry3K ( Lu et al., 2021 ) has 2,101 training and 500 of the 601 official test problems with numeric answers, where the teacher answers 57% correctly and concludes only 78% of its solutions within the 1,536-token budget. The correctness filter of SFT keeps 2,402 of the 3,000 ChartQA teacher samples (80%) and 1,163 of the 2,101 Geometry3K samples (55%), so an SFT budget of b b questions trains on about 0.8 ​ b 0.8b or 0.55 ​ b 0.55b demonstrations. Two out-of-distribution chart sets, 461 numeric questions from CharXiv ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and 500 factoid questions from ChartQAPro ( Masry et al., 2025 ) , score every ChartQA-trained model.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Every model sees the same prompt: solve step by step and end with a line Answer: <value> . Accuracy is measured using relaxed match with 5% numeric tolerance ( Methani et al., 2020 ) , the ChartQA convention, which we also apply to Geometry3K (the Geometry3K ordering is unchanged at 1% and 0.1%; Appendix I ). The stored records predate the evaluator’s stop-reason field, so truncation is inferred by re-tokenising the output (within 8 tokens of the budget; Appendix D ). For every correctness-filtered SFT and OPD model in the paper fewer than 1% of responses stop without an answer line, so an incomplete response is a truncated one (exceptions: the two SFT data controls of Section 4.3 , at 14% and 2% of responses at 300 problems). SFT runs 302 optimizer steps (two epochs of the full data) at every budget; OPD runs 150 steps of 16 rollouts at temperature 1.0 with a 512-token budget on charts and 1,536 on geometry; the step count is fixed within each method, not matched between them. Budgets b ∈ { 100,300,900 , 3000 } b\in\{100,300,900,3000\} questions (charts) or { 100,300,900 , 2101 } \{100,300,900,2101\} problems (geometry) are nested prefixes of a seeded shuffle. Seeds change the data order, rollout sampling, and LoRA initialisation; the test set is fixed; every point and every variant has four seeds. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Intervals.
sections.text: Every interval is a 95% question-clustered bootstrap interval: the 500 test questions are resampled with replacement, every seed’s outcome on a resampled question is kept together, and differences are paired by question within each seed and averaged over seeds; this treats the four trained models as fixed. For the headline comparisons we also give each seed’s difference and a t t interval over the four seeds, whose target is the method rather than these models (Appendix H ), and we call a difference robust only if the clustered and the seed-level interval both exclude zero.

sections.heading: Control: the training length of SFT.
sections.text: The protocol’s 302 steps are two epochs of the full data but about 20 epochs at 300 questions and 60 at 100, so the design could be handicapping SFT at low budgets. It is: retrained for 19, 38, 75, and 150 steps (Appendix K ), SFT peaks at 38 steps with 0.816 0.816 at 300 questions against 0.799 0.799 , and against it OPD’s lead shrinks to + 1.1 +1.1 [ − 0.6 -0.6 , + 2.8 +2.8 ] at 300 questions and + 1.5 +1.5 [ − 0.5 -0.5 , + 3.5 +3.5 ] at 100 (Table 1 ): OPD’s mean is above every SFT length, but its lead over a length-tuned SFT is 1 to 1.5 points and not robust, the tuned SFT’s seed spread is no larger than OPD’s, and the SFT length was selected on the test set, since the protocol has no validation split.

sections.heading: Is the teacher the source?
sections.text: Two observations point at the teacher. First, the teacher’s own solutions do not conclude: 78% of its training samples and 78% of its greedy test solutions contain an answer line. Second, the student’s failures concentrate on the problems the teacher does not finish (Appendix D ): on the 109 test problems the greedy teacher leaves incomplete, the zero-shot, SFT, and OPD students conclude 35%, 45%, and 20%; on the 391 it concludes, 73%, 85%, and 75%. Problem difficulty could drive both failures, so this is an association. The most direct evidence is what the teacher does when it takes over a student’s state (Table 4 , Appendix D ): continued greedily from a 256-token prefix of an OPD student’s truncated test output with the rest of the budget, it concludes 34%, and 3% from the truncation point, against 90% from a 256-token prefix of a concluded output. That budget shrinks with the cut (1,280, 1,024, 512, and 512 tokens), so the probe was repeated with 512 tokens at every cut (lower block): the within-trajectory difference between the 256-token cut and the truncation point falls from + 30.6 +30.6 [ + 25.4 +25.4 , + 35.8 +35.8 ] to + 12.2 +12.2 [ + 8.5 +8.5 , + 16.2 +16.2 ] points for the OPD student and to + 0.8 +0.8 [ − 5.1 -5.1 , + 7.4 +7.4 ] for the SFT student. At equal budget the teacher recovers few failed prefixes of either student (14% of SFT’s, 16% of OPD’s from 256 tokens) and most prefixes of concluded outputs (77 to 81%), but those are different problems and trajectories, so the probe describes the states rather than identifies what produced them. The teacher-forced probe agrees: along outputs that ran to the budget the teacher’s end-of-turn probability stays below 10 − 3 10^{-3} at every position, against 0.98 0.98 at the position where a concluded output stops, and its mass on answer-opening tokens (a proxy) peaks at 0.12 0.12 to 0.13 0.13 , against 0.63 0.63 to 0.82 0.82 where a concluded output’s answer line begins (Appendix D ). Changing the teacher’s prompt does not supply what is missing (Table 5 , on the zero-shot student’s failed prefixes from 300 training problems rather than the trained students’ test outputs): completion guidance leaves its completion at 19% against 18% ( + 1.1 +1.1 [ − 3.3 -3.3 , + 5.5 +5.5 ] points), and the gold answer lowers it to 7% ( − 11.0 -11.0 [ − 18.7 -18.7 , − 4.4 -4.4 ]), so no tested prompt establishes the improvement a training-level intervention would need.

sections.heading: Does a larger generation budget close the gap?
sections.text: It does not. Re-scoring the same four 900-problem models per method with 4,096 generated tokens instead of 1,536 (Appendix E ), the OPD students’ incomplete responses fall only from 186 to 168 of 500 (accuracy + 0.8 +0.8 [ − 0.4 -0.4 , + 1.9 +1.9 ]), whereas SFT’s fall from 120 to 50 (accuracy + 4.0 +4.0 [ + 2.5 +2.5 , + 5.5 +5.5 ]), so the gap widens from 7.6 7.6 to 10.8 10.8 points [ − 13.5 -13.5 , − 8.2 -8.2 ].

sections.heading: Which part of the filter matters: three SFT data sets.
sections.text: We retrained SFT on the teacher’s first sample for every problem, correct or not, concluded or not (Figure 3 a,b; Table 12 in Appendix F ). At 300 problems, where filtered SFT and OPD tie, removing the filter drops SFT’s completion rate to OPD’s 0.62 0.62 and its accuracy 1.8 1.8 points below both (intervals include zero). At 900 problems the unfiltered SFT is 3.6 3.6 points below the filtered one (per seed − 1.2 -1.2 to − 8.6 -8.6 , so the seed-level interval includes zero), its completion rate ( 0.69 0.69 ) lies between SFT’s and OPD’s, and it stays 4.2 4.2 points above OPD [ + 1.8 +1.8 , + 6.7 +6.7 ]. Removing the filter changes the demonstrations’ correctness, completeness, length, difficulty mix, and number at once. A third SFT, trained on the teacher’s first sample whenever it contains an answer line, correct or not (1,645 of 2,101 samples; the criterion is the answer line, not an emitted end-of-turn token), separates these: at 900 problems it reaches completion 0.74 0.74 and accuracy 0.473 0.473 , within 2.1 2.1 [ − 4.4 -4.4 , + 0.2 +0.2 ] and 0.8 0.8 [ − 3.2 -3.2 , + 1.6 +1.6 ] points of the correctness-filtered SFT and 4.7 4.7 [ + 2.5 +2.5 , + 6.9 +6.9 ] and 2.9 2.9 [ + 0.7 +0.7 , + 5.0 +5.0 ] points above the unfiltered one (Table 12 ; Appendix H ); at 300 problems it matches the filtered SFT ( 0.72 0.72 / 0.432 0.432 against 0.73 0.73 / 0.420 0.420 ). sections.heading: Three on-policy variants, and what their failure does and does not say about the objective.
sections.text: An on-policy analogue of the filter computes the loss only on rollouts that terminated (OPD-term); rollouts at the teacher’s temperature test the sampling distribution (OPD-t07); the forward KL tests whether the reverse KL attenuates the stopping signal (OPD-fwd). None of the three restores completion (Figure 3 a,b): it stays at 0.60 0.60 to 0.64 0.64 , accuracy within a point of plain OPD, and all three match plain OPD on ChartQA (Appendix J ). The gradient shows why the divergence alone cannot be blamed: the loss compares the two next-token distributions over the whole vocabulary at every position, so the teacher’s probability of stopping enters the loss whether or not the student sampled a stop. Writing p e p_{e} and q e q_{e} for the student’s and the teacher’s end-of-turn probabilities at a position, z e z_{e} for the student’s end-of-turn logit, and L L for the position’s reverse KL, ∂ L / ∂ z e = p e ​ ( log ⁡ ( p e / q e ) − L ) \partial L/\partial z_{e}=p_{e}\,(\log(p_{e}/q_{e})-L) , which pushes z e z_{e} up whenever log ⁡ ( p e / q e ) < L \log(p_{e}/q_{e})<L , that is p e < q e ​ e L p_{e}<q_{e}e^{L} (a student p e p_{e} below q e q_{e} suffices but is not necessary), but is scaled by p e p_{e} , so a student that rarely stops receives a small push; the forward KL has gradient p e − q e p_{e}-q_{e} , without the attenuation. That OPD-fwd fails as plain OPD does ( 0.394 0.394 , completion 0.60 0.60 ) argues against attenuation and leaves two candidates: the teacher, conditioned on the student’s overlong prefixes, may itself assign little probability to stopping; and the token-mean loss of Equation 1 is dominated by rollouts that ran to the budget, which hold about three quarters of the positions in the 900-problem runs (mean rollout length 892 tokens, termination rate 0.55 0.55 ). The second does not by itself explain the failure: a sequence-mean loss, in which every rollout counts once (OPD-seqmean; Appendix A ), does not restore completion, with 0.407 0.407 accuracy and 0.62 0.62 completion at 900 problems against 0.402 0.402 / 0.63 0.63 for plain OPD ( + 0.4 +0.4 [ − 1.4 -1.4 , + 2.1 +2.1 ] and − 0.7 -0.7 [ − 2.6 -2.6 , + 1.2 +1.2 ]; per seed in Appendix H ), the same termination trajectory during training, and 0.825 0.825 against 0.826 0.826 on ChartQA (Table 12 , Appendix J ). The first is what the probe above measures: q e q_{e} is below 10 − 3 10^{-3} on these prefixes, so the target the objective sets at these positions is a student that does not stop either. Whether the gradient at a position pushes z e z_{e} up depends on the student’s p e p_{e} and on the position’s full KL, neither of which we recorded, so the direction of the push is not measured: the probe establishes the target, not the gradient. Filtered SFT instead concentrates its supervision on demonstrations that contain an answer line.

sections.heading: On-policy feedback undoes the completion gain the student obtained from SFT.
sections.text: We started OPD from the merged filtered-SFT student of the same seed (OPD-sftinit), which concludes 76% of its test solutions, and trained it for the usual 150 steps. The training log (Figure 1 d) shows the behaviour being undone: the rollout termination rate is 0.79 0.79 over the first five steps, 0.54 0.54 by steps 21–40, and 0.60 0.60 over the rest of the run, against 0.63 0.63 , 0.48 0.48 , and 0.56 0.56 for plain OPD from the base model. At evaluation it concludes 62% of test responses, indistinguishable from plain OPD ( − 0.5 -0.5 [ − 2.8 -2.8 , + 1.7 +1.7 ]) and 13.8 13.8 points below the SFT model it started from ([ − 16.4 -16.4 , − 11.2 -11.2 ]; t t [ − 17.7 -17.7 , − 9.8 -9.8 ]). On the problems both it and SFT conclude no difference is detected ( − 0.5 -0.5 [ − 3.6 -3.6 , + 3.1 +3.1 ]); it ends at 0.422 0.422 , 5.9 5.9 points below SFT ([ − 8.2 -8.2 , − 3.8 -3.8 ]; t t [ − 10.9 -10.9 , − 1.0 -1.0 ]) and 1.9 1.9 above plain OPD ([ − 0.2 -0.2 , + 4.2 +4.2 ], not robust). The objective thus undoes a completion gain the student already had rather than merely failing to teach one; the experiment identifies the training process as the cause, not which part of it.

sections.heading: 4.4 Distribution shift and teacher size
sections.text: Off distribution (Appendix G ), both methods move the student by only 2 to 5 points on CharXiv and ChartQAPro, against a teacher that is itself at 0.41 0.41 there; the only paired difference that excludes zero is OPD’s + 3.0 +3.0 [ + 0.5 +0.5 , + 5.4 +5.4 ] on CharXiv at 100 questions, the other seven are within ± 0.7 \pm 0.7 points, and overlapping intervals do not establish equivalence. A 32B teacher on the 300-question ChartQA run (four seeds) is itself 1.4 1.4 points more accurate ( 0.858 0.858 against 0.844 0.844 , an interval that includes zero) and its student is not more accurate ( 0.812 0.812 against 0.826 0.826 , − 1.5 -1.5 [ − 3.1 -3.1 , + 0.2 +0.2 ]; + 1.2 +1.2 [ − 0.9 -0.9 , + 3.4 +3.4 ] against SFT).

sections.heading: On-policy distillation.
sections.text: Building on imitation-learning distillation ( Lin et al., 2020 ) , generalised knowledge distillation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , MiniLLM ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , and DistiLLM ( Ko et al., 2024 ) established student-sampled, teacher-scored token-level distillation, and Agarwal et al. (2024) reported the data-efficiency advantage that Section 4.1 measures for a VLM; text-only analyses ( Li et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) study its phenomenology. Concurrent text-only work argues that teacher reliability must be verified before dense on-policy supervision ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , that token-level corrections cannot unfold a complete repair ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , and that the teacher’s supervision is noisy ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) ; Qiu et al. (2026) show for visual hallucination that when teacher and student condition on the same flawed prefix the teacher’s signal collapses toward the student’s error. Ma (2026) shows that low teacher–student token-level divergence can coexist with an incorrect final answer in text-only OPD. We study a distinct failure mode in vision-language distillation: responses that never reach an answer line. We decompose the resulting accuracy gap by completion status and show that five on-policy variants fail to restore completion; OPD also erases the completion gain of an SFT-initialised student. Changing the divergence ( Xiao et al., 2026 , see also) or weighting rollouts (as Ai and Yan, 2026 , propose offline) did not restore completion.

sections.heading: On-policy distillation for vision-language models.
sections.text: A rapid 2026 literature adapts the objective to VLMs: visual-advantage weighting ( Liu et al., 2026 ) up-weights the tokens whose teacher prediction depends on fine visual detail and, trained on Geometry3K and ViRL39K, reports gains over plain OPD; decomposed gradient steering ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) and Fisher-projected distillation ( Xue et al., 2026 ) reshape the update toward grounding; others transfer reasoning from a text-only teacher ( Bousselham et al., 2026 ) or replace the teacher with the same model given privileged input ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . All change the objective and compare the change against plain OPD; we keep the objective fixed and ask how it compares with filtered demonstrations and which behaviour of the teacher the student acquires.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We study when OPD improves over filtered SFT and how teacher behavior on student-generated trajectories affects the student. OPD is data-efficient when the teacher reliably completes its solutions, but degrades when the teacher frequently fails to complete. On Geometry3K, most of the gap comes from incomplete responses, and OPD even erases completion gains previously learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT’s advantage, while teacher probes show that the teacher itself rarely completes from failed student trajectories. These results highlight teacher reliability on student-visited states as a critical factor in the success of OPD.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation covers one model family, two tasks, one student size below 4B, and a second teacher size on one task; other families, tasks, and scales remain untested. The attribution of the completion failure to the teacher rests on the teacher’s own trajectories, the per-problem overlap with the student’s failures, and the probe on the student’s prefixes; no tested teacher prompt clearly improved its recovery on the student’s failed prefixes (one lowered it), so a teacher trained to conclude from these states remains untested; we did not record the student’s own end-of-turn probability on those prefixes, and the continuation probe compares truncated and concluded outputs on different problems. With four seeds per point, several secondary differences depend on how the interval is formed (Appendix H ), and the SFT training length was selected on the test set. The unfiltered control removes both filters and its data carry an appended end-of-turn token; the completeness-only control separates the filters, not the token, and has more demonstrations. Truncation is inferred by re-tokenising (validated in Appendix D ); token roles are heuristic.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We used AI coding assistants (Claude, Anthropic) to assist in this project. It assisted with writing and refactoring training, evaluation, and analysis code under the authors’ direction, drafted the documentation and the prose of this manuscript, which the authors revised, and assisted with literature search. Every experiment was designed by the authors and run by them on their own compute; every number in the paper is read from the released per-question evaluation records, and the statistical procedures were checked against independent implementations in the test suite. The authors reviewed all generated code and text and take full responsibility for the content.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: We strictly adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics. This work distills publicly released models on public benchmarks and introduces no new data collection. The distilled students inherit the biases and failure modes of the teacher, which is one of the paper’s findings; we do not release them as general-purpose assistants.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: All code, configurations, Slurm scripts, per-step training logs, and per-question evaluation records (prediction, gold answer, correctness, and completion for every test question of every model) are released at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm ; every mean, interval, and paired difference in the paper is recomputed from the records by one script. Data order, rollout sampling, and LoRA initialisation are seeded, so a rerun follows the same recipe, but GPU kernels and vLLM decoding are not bit-reproducible across hardware, and re-evaluating the same weights can move a single seed’s accuracy by a few tenths of a point on ChartQA and by up to 2.8 2.8 points on Geometry3K (Section 3 ). The released evaluator records each generation’s stop reason and token count, which the records used here lack (Appendix D ). Appendix A lists every hyperparameter, the test-subset construction, the answer parser, and the end-of-turn convention; Appendix N lists the engineering choices needed to train a VLM student and teacher on one 40 GB GPU.

sections.heading: Prompts.
sections.text: Every model receives one image and the following user message (the ChartQA version replaces the first two sentences by “Look at the chart and answer the question below. Reason step by step: first read the relevant values from the chart, then do any calculation needed.”); the student always sees the geometry version. Look at the geometry figure and solve the problem below. Reason step by step: first state the given measures and relations you can read from the figure, then apply the relevant theorems and compute. Give the final answer as a number (decimals are fine; simplify radicals or fractions to a decimal if needed). [ guidance or paraphrase inserted here ]Keep the reasoning concise. On the last line, write the final answer in exactly this format: Answer: <your answer> Question: {question}[ privileged suffix appended here ] The completion guidance inserted before “Keep the reasoning concise” is: “Do not repeat a step you have already completed or restart the solution; once the value is determined, stop reasoning and commit to it, and always finish with the answer line.” The length-matched paraphrase replaces the first two sentences by “Study the geometry figure and work out the problem below. Proceed step by step: begin with the measures and relationships shown in the figure, then use the appropriate theorems to compute the result. Report the final answer as a number (decimals are acceptable; convert radicals or fractions to a decimal when needed).” and inserts “Name each quantity you use as you introduce it, so that the intermediate values of the solution can be read directly from the reasoning, and give the answer in the units of the figure.” at the same place. The privileged suffix is “The correct final answer is known to be: {answer}. sections.heading: How truncation is identified.
sections.text: The evaluation records used in this paper store each model’s output text but not the generator’s stop reason. Truncation is therefore inferred: the output is re-tokenised with the student’s tokenizer and counted as truncated if it lies within 8 tokens of the generation budget (the re-tokenised lengths of truncated outputs cluster at the budget minus 0 to 2 tokens; only one output in the 900-problem OPD runs falls between 8 and 40 tokens below it). “Stops” in Table 8 means not truncated by this criterion; it is an approximation of an emitted end-of-turn token, not a direct observation of one. The released evaluator now records the stop reason and output token count of every generation, so future records need no inference. Re-evaluating the 900-problem OPD and SFT students of seed 1 with that evaluator (models rebuilt from the Hub checkpoint and adapter; accuracy 0.422 0.422 and 0.486 0.486 against 0.406 0.406 and 0.472 0.472 in the recorded pass), the criterion agrees with the recorded stop reason on 500 of 500 and 498 of 500 responses: it calls 183 and 120 responses truncated, the generator 183 and 118; the two disagreements are SFT responses that stopped within 8 tokens of the budget, and no truncated response is missed.

sections.heading: Appendix N Engineering notes
sections.text: Training an 8B teacher and a 2B student together on one 40 GB GPU with full-vocabulary KL required: left-padded prompts so that generation positions align across the batch; logits_to_keep so that neither model materialises logits over the prompt or image tokens; the KL computed in fp32 in chunks over the sequence; micro-batching of the scoring pass with gradient accumulation; and rollouts at batch 16 (the rollout is 90% of step time and doubling its batch doubled throughput at constant peak memory of 27 GB). Checkpoints (adapter, optimizer, scheduler, data cursor) go to a remote repository every 25 steps and a killed job resumes from the latest one. vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) evaluates 500 questions in about 20 seconds. For a 32B teacher the student is pinned to one GPU and the teacher sharded over two more.

Kefei Yan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Yiren Wang 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Yiyang Wang 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Affiliation: Atlanta, GA, USA Email: {frank.yang,kyan66,ywang4361,ywang3420}@gatech.edu Abstract Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher’s supervision at each state affects the student’s learned behavior . To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT’s advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm . 1 Introduction Distilling a large vision-language model (VLM) into a small one is the standard way to make multimodal reasoning cheap enough to deploy. The common recipe is supervised fine-tuning on teacher-written solutions ( Magister et al., 2023 ; Ho et al., 2023 ) (SFT), which is behavior cloning: the student sees only states the teacher visited, drifts into others at inference, and its errors compound with sequence length ( Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ; Ross et al., 2011 ) . On-policy distillation (OPD) is the DAgger-style remedy ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) : the student samples its own solution, the teacher scores every generated token, and the student minimises a per-token divergence to the teacher on the states it actually reaches. For text-only language models, on-policy distillation on a twentieth of the training set has been reported to outperform supervised distillation on the full set ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , and it is now a standard post-training stage ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . A dense 2026 literature now adapts the objective to VLMs by re-weighting the teacher’s signal toward visually grounded tokens ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026 ) . While these methods change the objective and report the gains of the change, they leave open the question that comes first in practice: given a teacher and a few hundred to a few thousand training questions, when does plain on-policy feedback improve on filtered teacher demonstrations, and which behavior of the teacher does the student acquire along the way? Related work observes that teacher feedback degrades on flawed student prefixes ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) ; our experiments add completion as the behavior at stake, a matched comparison with filtered demonstrations, and a student that loses the completion gain it already had. The two recipes differ in cost and in what they transfer: OPD keeps the teacher in the loop and supervises the student on its own states with whatever the teacher does there; SFT pays once for teacher solutions and transfers only those that survive a correctness filter. Which difference dominates depends on the task, and in our experiments the wrong choice costs up to 7.9 7.9 points. Accuracy at a single budget cannot tell whether a gap comes from the amount of data or the number of training steps, from reasoning errors or from solutions that were never completed, from the objective or from the filter. To investigate these questions, we conducted (Section 2 ) a controlled comparison of the two channels across nested data budgets with each channel’s update count fixed, token-role divergence logging at every training step, and completion diagnostics, applied to a Qwen3-VL 2B student and 8B teacher ( Bai and others, 2025 ) on ChartQA ( Masry et al., 2022 ) and Geometry3K ( Lu et al., 2021 ) . Our contributions are threefold: • A controlled empirical comparison of OPD and filtered SFT. We systematically evaluate both training recipes across four data budgets, four seeds, and two vision-language reasoning tasks with different teacher completion rates. We further examine the sensitivity of their relative performance to SFT training length and evaluation distribution. • Identification of a completion-specific failure mode. We show that final-answer accuracy can obscure substantial differences in completion behavior. By decomposing accuracy differences according to whether each method produces a final answer, we characterize how incomplete responses contribute to the performance gap. We further demonstrate that continued OPD can undo completion behavior previously acquired through SFT. • An empirical investigation of the failure. We examine teacher behavior on student-generated prefixes, compare demonstrations filtered by correctness and completeness, and evaluate five OPD training variants. These analyses characterize the persistence of the completion failure and investigate the possible role of teacher feedback on student-visited states. Two findings stand out. • A persistent failure to complete solutions. On Geometry3K, where the teacher itself does not finish 22% of its solutions within the token budget, OPD students at 900 problems conclude 63% of test responses against 76% for SFT and trail SFT by 7.9 7.9 points ( − 10.5 -10.5 to − 5.3 -5.3 ), of which 6.6 6.6 points come from problems that only one method concludes. OPD started from the SFT student returns its rollout termination rate to plain OPD’s within 40 steps and ends at 62% test completion, the zero-shot level. • A small, non-robust data-efficiency advantage with a reliable teacher. On ChartQA, OPD with 300 training questions reaches 0.826 0.826 accuracy, within 1.4 1.4 points of SFT trained on 3,000 ( 0.840 0.840 ), and leads SFT by 2.7 2.7 points at the same budget under the protocol’s fixed SFT length (per seed + 0.6 +0.6 to + 5.8 +5.8 ) and by 1.1 1.1 to 1.5 1.5 points, with intervals that include zero, against an SFT whose training length is tuned. Together, these results characterize a previously underexplored failure mode of on-policy distillation and give a working rule and a target: on these tasks OPD was competitive with filtered SFT at small budgets only where the teacher reliably completed its solutions; where it did not, the student’s completion failures concentrated on the problems the teacher does not finish, and from those prefixes the teacher rarely concludes, even with the answer in its prompt. Whether that causes the failure or accompanies it awaits a teacher trained to conclude from such states (Section 4.3 ). The case for on-policy supervision is DAgger’s ( Ross and Bagnell, 2010 ; Ross et al., 2011 ) : querying the expert on the learner’s own states removes the compounding error of behavior cloning, provided the expert’s action on those states is worth imitating. The two channels therefore differ in two things at once: the states on which the teacher is queried (its own prefixes against the student’s) and the teacher behavior that reaches the student (only correct solutions against everything the teacher does). Our design separates these. 2.2 Design: what is held fixed and what varies Rather than propose a new objective, we hold everything but the supervision channel and the amount of data fixed: one frozen teacher and one student initialisation, with LoRA on the language-model projections and the vision encoder frozen, so the channels differ in language-side supervision and not in visual representation; one prompt, answer format, generation budget, scorer, and held-out test set per task; budgets that are nested prefixes of one seeded shuffle, so both channels see the same questions and a larger budget adds questions rather than replacing them; and a number of optimizer updates that is fixed within each channel whatever the budget, so that along a curve only the amount of data changes (the counts are not matched between channels; a training-length control on SFT checks this). The teacher is neither prompted for completeness nor retrained: its reliability varies only through the task, and two tasks on which the same teacher is reliable and unreliable turn that dependence into a difference between tasks rather than between teachers. The channel (filtered demonstrations against on-policy token-level feedback) is crossed with four budgets, two tasks, and four paired seeds. Because the channel bundles the state distribution with the filter, two further SFT data sets (no filter; every teacher sample with an answer line, correct or not) separate the two. Five single-component interventions on OPD (the loss on terminated rollouts only, the teacher’s sampling temperature, the forward KL, a sequence-mean loss, initialisation from the SFT student) change one part of the recipe each, and a larger teacher and two out-of-distribution test sets check the dependence on teacher size and test distribution. 2.3 What we measure Beyond accuracy, three complementary analyses characterize the observed differences and probe possible explanations. Completion diagnostics : a response is complete if it contains an answer line (one without counts as wrong), terminates if it emits the end-of-turn token before the budget, and is truncated if it reaches the budget; paired accuracy differences are decomposed by which method concluded the problem. Feedback logging : at every OPD step we record each generated token’s divergence and a heuristic role ( answer line , numeric value , arithmetic , text ); a role’s KL concentration is its share of the batch’s divergence divided by its share of tokens. Teacher probes : the teacher is continued greedily from prefixes of the student’s truncated and concluded outputs and its end-of-turn probability is read along them, to ask what it does on the student’s states rather than on its own. 3 Experimental setup Models and tasks. Is the teacher the source? Two observations point at the teacher. First, the teacher’s own solutions do not conclude: 78% of its training samples and 78% of its greedy test solutions contain an answer line. Second, the student’s failures concentrate on the problems the teacher does not finish (Appendix D ): on the 109 test problems the greedy teacher leaves incomplete, the zero-shot, SFT, and OPD students conclude 35%, 45%, and 20%; on the 391 it concludes, 73%, 85%, and 75%. Problem difficulty could drive both failures, so this is an association. Building on imitation-learning distillation ( Lin et al., 2020 ) , generalised knowledge distillation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , MiniLLM ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , and DistiLLM ( Ko et al., 2024 ) established student-sampled, teacher-scored token-level distillation, and Agarwal et al. (2024) reported the data-efficiency advantage that Section 4.1 measures for a VLM; text-only analyses ( Li et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) study its phenomenology. Concurrent text-only work argues that teacher reliability must be verified before dense on-policy supervision ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , that token-level corrections cannot unfold a complete repair ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , and that the teacher’s supervision is noisy ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) ; Qiu et al. (2026) show for visual hallucination that when teacher and student condition on the same flawed prefix the teacher’s signal collapses toward the student’s error. Ma (2026) shows that low teacher–student token-level divergence can coexist with an incorrect final answer in text-only OPD. We study a distinct failure mode in vision-language distillation: responses that never reach an answer line. We decompose the resulting accuracy gap by completion status and show that five on-policy variants fail to restore completion; OPD also erases the completion gain of an SFT-initialised student. Changing the divergence ( Xiao et al., 2026 , see also) or weighting rollouts (as Ai and Yan, 2026 , propose offline) did not restore completion. On-policy distillation for vision-language models. A rapid 2026 literature adapts the objective to VLMs: visual-advantage weighting ( Liu et al., 2026 ) up-weights the tokens whose teacher prediction depends on fine visual detail and, trained on Geometry3K and ViRL39K, reports gains over plain OPD; decomposed gradient steering ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) and Fisher-projected distillation ( Xue et al., 2026 ) reshape the update toward grounding; others transfer reasoning from a text-only teacher ( Bousselham et al., 2026 ) or replace the teacher with the same model given privileged input ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . All change the objective and compare the change against plain OPD; we keep the objective fixed and ask how it compares with filtered demonstrations and which behaviour of the teacher the student acquires. 6 Conclusion We study when OPD improves over filtered SFT and how teacher behavior on student-generated trajectories affects the student. OPD is data-efficient when the teacher reliably completes its solutions, but degrades when the teacher frequently fails to complete. On Geometry3K, most of the gap comes from incomplete responses, and OPD even erases completion gains previously learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT’s advantage, while teacher probes show that the teacher itself rarely completes from failed student trajectories. These results highlight teacher reliability on student-visited states as a critical factor in the success of OPD. Limitations Our evaluation covers one model family, two tasks, one student size below 4B, and a second teacher size on one task; other families, tasks, and scales remain untested. The attribution of the completion failure to the teacher rests on the teacher’s own trajectories, the per-problem overlap with the student’s failures, and the probe on the student’s prefixes; no tested teacher prompt clearly improved its recovery on the student’s failed prefixes (one lowered it), so a teacher trained to conclude from these states remains untested; we did not record the student’s own end-of-turn probability on those prefixes, and the continuation probe compares truncated and concluded outputs on different problems. With four seeds per point, several secondary differences depend on how the interval is formed (Appendix H ), and the SFT training length was selected on the test set. The unfiltered control removes both filters and its data carry an appended end-of-turn token; the completeness-only control separates the filters, not the token, and has more demonstrations.
